chapters.description:
Abacus 3 is the native 32-bit Artemis spreadsheet and analysis line. Sparse worksheets and schema-defined formatted-table tabs coexist with multiple tabs, cross-tab references, typed columns, virtual calculated columns, unique-key lookups and a documented read-only SQL subset. Disk-backed columnar storage uses column pruning, conservative statistics-based skipping and dataset-dependent encoding rather than promised compression or throughput.

Reports extend earlier spreadsheet-field layouts with one-off/repeating sections and graphical {chart_types} charts. Capability-aware preview includes titles, axes and legends while retaining standard TUI editing and monochrome patterns. Supported printer drivers paginate output; refresh stale query/formula results before printing.

Embedded Pulse uses the Abacus-owned document API; standalone Pulse retains exclusive offline access to supported closed files. Preserve formulas and invalidate changed cached results rather than allowing a second concurrent writer.

Versioned SSG summaries remain independent planning inputs with decimal checks and reconciliation, without ledger write-back or a live database link. CSV import maps schemas, quoting, delimiters, encodings, dates, decimal conventions, nulls and text identifiers, with rejected-record diagnostics. Value-only export explicitly loses formulas and types.

VSAM import consumes host-exported sequential logical records, for example through IDCAMS REPRO, with a supplied record layout and transfer path. Declare boundaries, lengths, offsets and keys; convert EBCDIC, supported binary, packed decimal and zoned decimal explicitly. Raw VSAM images, clusters and indexes are not desktop interchange files. Reject unsupported layouts without reinterpretation. Preserve older document versions; older Abacus/Pulse editions must reject unsupported new features before writing.

The initial release uses flat formatted tables. Bounded nested arrays/maps/structs with explicit aggregation/expansion and broader Lotus 1-2-3 response features are later work. It does not promise background recalculation, unlimited documents/memory, a full transactional SQL database, arbitrary VSAM image access or unrestricted nested data.

Qualify actual Artemis 128/256 KiB and later PRO configurations separately. Measure memory, storage, timing, I/O and compression on named datasets; larger jobs may need expansion or disk-backed processing. Exercise sales import, customer/product joins, margins, regional grouping, printed charts, save/reopen and the equivalent Pulse script. Check conversions, rounding, nulls, duplicate keys, join cardinality, cancellation, grouped undo, visibility, dependency invalidation, recovery and unsupported-version rejection. No unmeasured minimum RAM or maximum row count is asserted.

chapters.description:
AIONix2 develops {baseline_os_id} for {processor_architecture_id}, retaining {portable_api_id}. The initial release combines executable system ROM, documented legacy ABI compatibility, protected preemptive user processes, recoverable HDD storage, users/permissions, a POSIX-oriented subset and an event-driven TUI foundation.

ROM execution/ABI, resilient multitasking and recoverable storage are essential, followed by access enforcement and the staged interface/UI work. Paging, metadata journaling, broader networking, threads/locales and a full windowed GUI remain later work, not initial release gates. These are engineering priorities rather than completed qualification.

Stable kernel code, core libraries, a small shell/basic utilities and recovery tools share read-only, cacheable executable ROM; each process keeps writable state in DRAM. The replaceable system cartridge supplies at least {minimum_os_rom_bytes} bytes. EEPROM BIOS remains boot/diagnostic firmware; optional services, larger utilities and patches load from disk rather than copying the entire ROM into RAM.

Executable ABI versions select legacy adapters, stable library dispatch and capability discovery. Preserve documented ERA instruction semantics, C calling conventions and layouts, syscall entry/numbers, loading, errors and legacy signals. Privileged drivers, undocumented kernel assumptions and direct hardware access need separate qualification; Z80 C code must be recompiled. Versioned dispatch and page-sized RAM overlays patch code after ROM checksum/version checks, with recovery boot bypassing disk patches. A qualified minor revision can be installed by exchanging a host-compatible cartridge.

The preferred DRAM allocation is {preferred_dram_bytes} bytes; the 256 KiB minimum is an engineering fit target, not a measured guarantee, and the server retains its existing 1 MiB configuration. Illustrative allocations are 40 KiB for kernel state/tables/stacks, 24 KiB for filesystem buffers, 16 KiB for translation metadata, 12 KiB for terminal/UI input, 20 KiB for services/patch reserve and 144 KiB for applications. Shared ROM, sparse page tables, small kernel stacks and reliable copy-on-write reduce demand. Allocation failure must be handled; ROM cannot replace writable RAM. Later swap requires qualified restart, locking and I/O with fault handlers resident, and should address occasional pressure rather than routine oversizing.

A compact monolithic kernel timer-preempts user processes while bounding non-preemptible kernel critical sections. Priority aging, sleeping I/O and atomic sleep/wakeup provide fairness; short interrupts defer work. Validate user pointers, protect kernel/device mappings, constrain per-process memory/files/requests, bound driver retries and timeouts, and retain responsive administrative termination. Process exit cleans files, memory, locks and child state. Kernel-controlled DMA uses checked pinned buffers; process isolation alone protects neither kernel/driver faults nor DMA. A fully preemptible kernel and application threads are not initial requirements.

A versioned inode filesystem separates directory entries from metadata, using {allocation_block_bytes}-byte blocks and {block_identifier_bits}-bit block IDs. The initial qualification range is {qualification_volume_mb} MB, not a capacity ceiling or bundled-drive change. Direct/indirect pointers, metadata timestamps/link counts, bounded caches, mounts and logical-sector drivers with CHS translation support the layout.

Clean/dirty state, a consistency checker, ordered metadata writes, explicit synchronization and tested backup/restore establish recoverability. Exact disk format/limits, file-offset and timestamp representation, legacy import/mount behaviour and controller persistence guarantees remain open. A later small metadata journal still needs power-loss/write-order testing and does not alone ensure application-data durability.

Numeric users/groups, owner/group/other permissions including directory search, creation masks, real/effective credentials and login/home directories define access. Protect salted, costed password hashes within CPU budgets and enforce permissions on every relevant kernel operation. Device/mount/configuration administration and audit records are protected. Qualify credential/exec transitions before enabling set-user-ID programs; servers authenticate users rather than trusting supplied UIDs. Extended ACLs are later work.

The initial subset defines file/descriptor operations and errors; descriptor duplication/inheritance; copy-on-write fork, exec, wait, status and environment; signals/masks/dispositions and interruption; canonical/raw terminals and foreground process groups; hierarchical paths, working directories and hard/symbolic links; pipes, EOF/broken-pipe handling and readiness multiplexing; shell quoting, redirection, pipelines, variables and statuses; wall and monotonic clocks with explicit timestamp formats. Publish an implemented/partial/absent matrix and unsupported-operation errors rather than claiming conformance from names. Efficient spawn, broader file control/mapping, full job control/pseudo-terminals, sockets/IPC, utilities, locales, threads and timers are later additions.

Applications own business logic and semantic Open/Save/Select/Cancel commands. A shared abstraction provides events, menus, forms, lists, focus, layout, measurement and drawing contexts; translation adapters preserve TUI, terminal, device and legacy ABI behaviour above native process/file/IPC/timer/input/display services. These are logical library/service layers, not four mandatory processes or IPC hops.

A bounded event queue handles keys, timers, focus, redraw and future pointer events. Opaque view/window handles initially describe text regions; clipping, invalidation, repaint, layout constraints and text measurement use separate cell/pixel coordinates. Clipboard/selection ownership is bounded, and graphics/font/colour/pointer support is discovered by version and capability. Compact text state, dirty regions and redraw callbacks avoid a mandatory full-screen backing bitmap. A later GUI can host old character applications in terminal windows without automatically redesigning them.

Release tests must cover legacy binary regressions, fairness/termination under CPU load, injected faults and cleanup, concurrent disk/terminal/DMA I/O, power loss and durable saves, credentials/permissions, measured ROM/RAM use with Abacus/compiler/server workloads, and TUI fallback/legacy terminal behaviour.

chapters.description:
The system adapts {base_version} for banked-ROM execution while preserving standard entry points, loading conventions and available-memory boundaries. A single foreground application can use ordinary CP/M console/file services; richer behaviour uses the separate versioned Logix API.

The CCP interprets commands and loads disk/cartridge programs; BDOS supplies file services through the machine BIOS, which adapts calls to Logix drivers. Motherboard ROM supplies {firmware_contents}. The system cartridge supplies {cartridge_contents}; command buffers and mutable system state remain in RAM. ROM constants/code must be separated from state and self-modifying routines adapted.

In conventional CP/M, 0000H–00FFH holds vectors, default file-control data and the command/disk buffer. Programs load at {program_load_address} in the transient program area and call BDOS through {bdos_entry}; CCP, BDOS and BIOS occupy higher memory. The TPA is application RAM, not an OS module. Transient editor/copy/assembler/debugger/maintenance utilities load when needed.

Compared with 1.3, the 1.4 base supports four logical drives, BIOS sector translation and extra drive state; BDOS begins one 256-byte page lower while CCP/BIOS bases stay fixed. It revises disk errors, returns DE consistently with HL and splits BDOS into PL/M logic plus an assembly interface. Vanilla 1.4 does not contain Logix banked-ROM, cartridge, dynamic-driver, TUI/clipboard/workspace services or the later CP/M 2.0 disk-parameter-block model.

Logix boot firmware discovers cartridges and provides diagnostics/recovery. The common-memory runtime preserves accessible entry code, stack and interrupt state across nested bank switches, following {memory_model_id}. Drivers in motherboard/device ROM or extensions register video, keyboard, floppy and FlexiBUS services. BIOS and relevant BDOS assumptions must match Aurelia disk formats. DMA uses physical-bank descriptors, bounded transfers and ready handshakes; drain or abort it before warm boot or buffer reuse. Video uploads expose dedicated sprite SRAM and atomic descriptors with backpressure, falling back to programmed I/O where needed.

Screen services query usable dimensions, clip/scroll and distinguish document from display coordinates. Compact 40-column and expanded 80-column layouts fit dialogs, names and errors; semantic text/selection/warning roles map to colour or monochrome. Structured character, function/navigation and modifier events support blocking or polled input. Shared fields, lists, menus, forms, popups and focus movement use consistent editing and clipboard commands. Clipboard formats, lengths, capacity, ownership and errors are explicit. Contexts are created/destroyed and activated/deactivated with redraw; one may cover the whole screen. System timing and repeat replace CPU-speed loops.

Sequential applications can use these services without multitasking. Exact widgets, clipboard capacity and workspace reservations remain implementation choices. Preserve legacy console behaviour and stable target ABI, use capability discovery, and avoid hard-coded stride, video addresses, last columns or hardware registers. The same documented API spans Aurelia, Aurelia+ and Artemis; Artemis mediates shared display/clipboard access between processes.

chapters.description: AION C IDE integrates source editing, project/module configuration, compilation, assembly, linking, diagnostics and debugging. The editor highlights C keywords, comments, string/character literals and preprocessor lines using semantic attributes. Monochrome displays use distinguishable supported intensity/inverse attributes; selection and error emphasis remain readable. Lexical recoloring is restricted to affected visible text with bounded state for multiline comments. Disk-backed buffers support sources larger than editor working memory. Tools may execute sequentially and use overlays, preserving source, cursor and diagnostic state.

The compiler implements {language_contract_id} and libraries follow {runtime_contract_id}. Structures, typedef, function pointers, documented 32-bit integer arithmetic and shared string/stream-I/O semantics are retained. Profiles {build_profiles} build {build_targets}; later ANSI C features and future processor targets are not implied. The project records modules, include paths, libraries and debug/size/speed options, rebuilds changed modules and maps diagnostics back to source locations.

The Z80 optimizer performs constant folding and propagation, provably safe dead/unreachable-code elimination, local common-expression elimination, redundant load/store removal, branch simplification and target-specific peephole optimization. Basic-block liveness and register-pair allocation reduce memory traffic. Loop address induction and strength reduction are used when profitable; small visible function bodies may be selectively inlined under size/speed policy. Aliasing, external/assembly calls, signed arithmetic and hardware effects constrain transformations. Driver calls and declared hardware accesses are treated as observable effects. Assembly interface declarations must expose clobbers and side effects or the compiler assumes conservative barriers. No full modern whole-program optimizer is promised. Compare optimized and unoptimized outputs for identical numeric and I/O behaviour.

Performance-critical block copying/filling, string scanning/comparison, integer arithmetic, selected decimal/fixed-point operations and record comparison/search kernels are implemented in tuned Z80 assembly. Publish operation widths, precision, rounding, overflow, overlap and error rules. Link only referenced library modules; application data and writable runtime state remain in RAM. Users can assemble their own modules, create libraries and link them with C objects. Publish symbols, object/archive format, argument/return locations, preserved registers, stack rules, data layout and callback/reentrancy requirements. Supply C-to-assembly, assembly-to-C and callback examples. Interrupt handlers do not reenter non-reentrant CP/M/TUI routines. Benchmark useful operations including call and bank-switch overhead; no blanket speed or code-size guarantee.

Headers, ROM-call stubs and examples use the accepted system-cartridge TUI. Provide text fields, lists, tables, dropdown selection and buttons with consistent validation, Tab/Shift-Tab focus traversal, keyboard shortcuts, selection and copy/cut/paste. DRI owns shared clipboard storage/lifecycle; helpers obey published capacity, formats and ownership. The IDE SDK supplies composite table/dropdown helpers over existing ROM primitives when a native control is absent; this does not silently add new services to the accepted ROM image. Tables request bounded rows/pages through application callbacks. Forms use C-defined descriptors and callbacks; a visual drag-and-drop form designer is not part of this release.

Use {display_api} to enumerate/test/select modes and query the actual configuration. Text mode is the compact default for the IDE; generated applications can draw text/glyphs, lines, rectangles, fills and documented bitmap formats with clipping. SDK adapters render the same control model in text or bitmap mode with shared keyboard semantics; optional helper code links into the application rather than assuming every renderer is in ROM. Bitmap rendering is limited to qualified modes and memory budgets. Mode changes preserve application document/control state and trigger redraw. Do not assume simultaneous text and full bitmap buffers, readable 80 columns on every monitor, transparent conversion of old programs or hardware drawing acceleration.

Provide symbol maps, emitted source/line-to-address mappings, inspectable RAM state, RAM breakpoints and single-step for qualified builds. Optimized code may reorder or remove source operations; use debug builds for predictable stepping. XIP ROM cannot be patched with software breakpoints: use supported call stubs or qualified RAM-loaded equivalents. ROM-aware linking separates code/constants from initialized and uninitialized RAM data, provides disk/cartridge images and reports ROM/RAM usage and stack estimates. Indirect calls, recursion and assembly routines can prevent a proven stack bound and must be flagged.

Supported hosts are {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}, using {runtime_cpm_aurelia}; the nominal installed-RAM minimum remains {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The 48 KiB profile publishes 40704 application bytes and the 64 KiB profile 57088 bytes under the existing reservations. These are ceilings, not spare space available to every tool. Measure editor buffers, pass overlays, library state, stack and disk intermediate files against actual reservations. A single-drive workflow may require media exchanges. Two distribution diskettes follow the recorded package definition, with image fit, working-disk requirements and installation qualification still required. No additional RAM or ROM capacity is inferred.

Qualify syntax coloring and recovery from unterminated comments/strings, diagnostic navigation, incremental builds, library selection, C/assembly calls and nested bank restoration. Compare debug/optimized arithmetic and file results; test overlap, rounding, overflow and invalid inputs. Exercise forms and bitmap redraw in 40/80-column and monochrome/color configurations, clipboard-full, disk-full and exhausted-memory failures. Benchmark forms/record entry, sorting/search, decimal accounting and a bounded recalculation workload on named hardware. Report executable size, peak workspace, stack estimates, disk scratch use and build/run times. Fast libraries and advanced optimization are implementation commitments; measured superiority to earlier tools or hand-written assembly remains to be demonstrated. SSG General Ledger is an external acceptance workload: reconcile CBASIC and C financial results, measure native application work and ROM TUI overhead separately, and keep the publisher’s source and accounting rules outside the reusable IDE product.
